facts.statement: The genus Diogenornis was described in 1983 by Brazilian scientist Herculano Marcos Ferraz de Alvarenga from fossils found in the Itaboraí Formation in southeastern Brazil.
facts.quote: It was described in 1983 by Brazilian scientist Herculano Marcos Ferraz de Alvarenga based on fossils found in the Itaboraí Formation in southeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: Diogenornis lived from the Middle Paleocene to the Early Eocene.
facts.quote: Diogenornis is an extinct genus of ratites, that lived from the Middle Paleocene to the Early Eocene (Riochican to Casamayoran in the SALMA classification).

facts.statement: Diogenornis grew to about two-thirds the size of the modern greater rhea, reaching a height of approximately 90 cm.
facts.quote: It grew to about two thirds the size of the modern greater rhea, at about 90 cm of height.

facts.statement: Although initially classified in the family Opisthodactylidae, further examination showed Diogenornis was more similar to the modern rhea.
facts.quote: While initially considered a member of the family Opisthodactylidae, further examination of the fossil remains showed that it was more similar to the modern rhea.

facts.statement: Recent phylogenetic studies suggest Diogenornis has a closer affiliation to Australian ratites, such as cassowaries and emus.
facts.quote: However, recent phylogenetic studies have shown a closer affiliation to Australian ratites, the cassowaries and emus.

facts.statement: Diogenornis possessed a narrow beak similar to tinamous, lithornithids, and cassowaries, along with rather large wings.
facts.quote: Diogenornis possesses a rather narrow beak, similar to that of tinamous, lithornithids and cassowaries, as well as rather large wings.

facts.statement: The unspecialized traits of Diogenornis suggest it had recently evolved from a flying ancestor.
facts.quote: These traits, both rather unspecialised, seem to suggest a then recent development from a flying ancestor.

facts.statement: The presence of Diogenornis expands the known range of this clade to the South American Paleocene, well before the appearance of Emuarius.
facts.quote: This may reevaluate the origins and distribution of this clade, expanding their range to the South American Paleocene, well before the appearance of Emuarius.

facts.statement: Diogenornis co-existed with early rheas, indicating very high ratite diversity in South America during the Paleogene.
facts.quote: Recent findings nonetheless show that it co-existed with early rheas, meaning the ratite diversity of South America was very high during the Paleogene.

facts.statement: Diogenornis is classified within the superorder Palaeognathae and the order Casuariiformes.
The time range for Diogenornis is the Ypresian, from 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Ypresian (56 to 48.07 million years ago)

rejected.statement: According to Gerald Mayr, Diogenornis is best considered a stem-group member of the family Rheidae.
rejected.quote: According to Gerald Mayr, Diogenornis is best considered a stem-group member of the Rheidae.
